changes.after: A string can take more bytes in storage than the number of characters you read.

before: A Ruby String stores bytes with an encoding label. In UTF-8, bytesize counts storage bytes and length counts characters, so an accented character may occupy multiple bytes. Neither measure is a universal count of visible grapheme clusters.

encode converts representation when possible; force_encoding only changes how existing bytes are interpreted. valid_encoding? checks whether bytes fit the label. Do not silently relabel corrupted external data as valid text.

encode receives a target encoding name and returns a converted String. In this ASCII example UTF-16LE needs two bytes for A; converting back recovers the text.
```ruby
text = "A"
converted = text.encode("UTF-16LE")
puts converted.bytesize
puts converted.encode("UTF-8")
```
It prints:
```text
2
A
```

force_encoding receives an encoding label and changes that same String's label without converting its bytes. dup first gives this example a separate mutable String. Relabeling its UTF-8 bytes for é as US-ASCII leaves two bytes that are invalid under the new label.
```ruby
text = "é".dup
text.force_encoding("US-ASCII")
puts text.bytesize
puts text.valid_encoding?
```
It prints:
```text
2
false
```

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:

```ruby
puts text.bytesize
puts text.length
puts text.valid_encoding?

```

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
text = "é"
puts text.bytesize
puts text.length
puts text.valid_encoding?
```
The output is `2`, then `1`, then `true`. Length counts one character, and the encoding check says the bytes form valid text.
